# October 27 and 28: Designing the Schematic

![Screenshot 2026-10-28 at 5.19.01 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/8e2c38d64131d6c350c1fce737f84a018de1860b22b4a419561f3b11d231027b.png)

This week I'll be designing a virtual sandbox, a simple fidget toy where each pixel on an OLED screen represents a grain of sand, and you can move it around through motion. Before actually starting, I had an idea for how I would go about designing this project. I would use the classic 0.96" OLED screen and make sure it is single-colored for uniformity. I also needed an accelerometer to track the motion, so I decided on the LIS3DH. It's relatively cheap, small enough for the project, and has lots of documentation online so I can learn how to program it. For the microcontroller, I'm using the ESP32-S3, the same chip I used in my Bee Board project from last week. I already have some experience with it, so that should make designing just a little bit easier.

For the schematic, I first added the chip, then I added a 1x4 generic connector to represent the OLED and a 1x8 connector to represent the accelerometer. I searched up the order of pins of each component and considered the orientation I want to make sure I wire the parts correctly. Then, I added a button, but I'm not too sure what I'll do with it yet. I'm considering making it a reset button, or maybe even something that changes the mode.

After finding and adding all the footprints, I still felt like something was missing, and then I realized that I should make the sandbox portable. I thought that I would have to rethink my entire project, but it turns out that the bottom of my board actually has some solder pads for a battery. I had learn a little bit about batteries as I went because this is the first project that I'm working with them.

I thought that it would be kind of impractical to have a device that's constantly on, so I added a toggle switch so I can shut it off whenever I like. I'm pretty proud of the way I did this: I added a 1x1 connector for the  battery's positive wire to go in, and that leads to the toggle switch on the PCB, and that leads to another 1x1 connector where I can attach another wire that'll go directly to the solder pad on the ESP32. By making it like this, the switch can be fixed in place.

![Screenshot 2026-10-28 at 5.19.39 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/d3d5cbe4adb842f00018ceae0fb4096984221728cff37c1bb21871a667a2a901.png)

![Screenshot 2026-10-28 at 5.20.50 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/828fb4739999647a86b38ed4519cdd8044f011368d50d9d8151e9191996c1f1a.png)

There's a big problem that needs fixing when I design my PCB though. The battery pads are on the other side of the board, so I won't be able to access them if I lay the ESP32 flush against the PCB. I'm debating between two solutions: adding a cutout on the PCB itself, or finding a way to raise the board so that I can access it from below.

Next I'll work on that, and then after I'll tackle the firmware.

# tl;dr: I finished designing the schematic for my virtual sandbox. I added the connectors for the OLED and accelerometer, and later I decided to add a battery and a toggle switch. I had to do some research on how to do this. I came up with a good solution to mount the switch on the PCB and have wires that go in/out of 1x1 connectors. I need to find out a way for me to connect the battery wires to the underside of the microcontroller, which is what I plan to tackle next.
